vignette: David, a 56-year-old musician, had once found joy in the rhythm of life, but a traumatic event had shattered his sense of safety and trust. The assault, which occurred five years ago at a music festival, left him with vivid memories of violence amidst the carefree atmosphere. He could still recall the scent of a specific cologne worn by his attacker, a fragrance that now triggered overwhelming dread whenever he encountered it. These triggers, like the scent of cologne, ignited memories that flooded him with a renewed sense of threat; each encounter felt like a reminder that danger could reemerge at any moment. Each time the scent wafted by, his body reacted instinctively, flooding him with a sense of impending danger that made his heart race and his palms sweat, as if he were reliving the terror of the assault. It was as if the world had shifted; every instance of blood, whether in a scene from a movie or a minor injury he witnessed, sent him spiraling back to that moment of terror. The mere thought of being in a crowded place where sudden movements could occur made him feel vulnerable, as if danger lurked around every corner. Each time he felt that vulnerability rise, it pulled memories of the assault to the forefront of his mind, as if his body was reminding him of the danger he had experienced. In the years following the assault, David had developed a rigid routine, confining himself to a limited number of places where he felt somewhat secure, often his home or a quiet corner in a familiar café. This avoidance of wider spaces and social situations had inadvertently created a web of triggers; every familiar corner became a reminder of what he had lost, reinforcing his isolation while also keeping the memories close to the surface. Outside of these sanctuaries, he was consumed by irritability, snapping at his wife and friends for minor issues, feeling as though he was perpetually on edge. Authority figures, especially those in uniforms, evoked a deep-seated fear within him, compelling him to avoid interactions at all costs. The sense of threat that accompanied these encounters was palpable; he felt that any interaction could lead to a resurgence of the trauma, reinforcing his need to escape even the slightest confrontation. He had come to believe that expressing anger was a weakness; he never allowed himself to feel or show it, which only added to his internal turmoil. Instead, he suppressed his emotions, a strategy that left him feeling detached and unfulfilled. David's memories of the event were fragmented. The disjointed recollections haunted him, often surfacing unexpectedly and leading him to employ maladaptive strategies like isolating himself from friends, as he sought to evade the pain they invoked. Some moments were strikingly clear, as if they were etched into his mind, while others remained shrouded in mystery, blank spaces that he could not fill. This inconsistency in his memory led to further confusion and frustration; he often found himself pushing thoughts away before he could fully grasp them, hoping to shield himself from the pain they invoked. He had lost the ability to tell a coherent story of what had happened, both to others and to himself. This fragmentation of memory was compounded by his avoidance; the more he steered clear of discussing the event, the more intense and disjointed the memories became, almost as if they were waiting to break free and overwhelm him. Each time he avoided recalling the event, he found the memories would surge back with greater intensity, making it feel as though the danger he had once faced was still present, urging him to retreat further into isolation. Each time he attempted to recount the event, he was left with a jumbled narrative that only deepened his feelings of helplessness and loss. As David navigated his daily life, he encountered triggers that heightened his sense of threat. With every reminder of the assault, he felt an overwhelming urgency to flee situations that could bring those memories crashing back, confirming his belief that the world was inherently dangerous. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, amplifying his anxiety and making him hyper-aware of his surroundings." The smell of cologne would remind him of the assault, making his heart race and his palms sweat. As he recalled the moment of the attack, even the faintest scent would prompt him to scan his environment for threats, each whiff reinforcing his belief that he was surrounded by danger. Any sudden movement by those around him would send him into a defensive posture, instantly putting him on guard. It was as if his body had forgotten how to relax; the tension coursed through him, reinforcing his belief that the world was a dangerous place. This heightened threat perception further complicated his ability to engage with his memories, as he often felt overwhelmed by emotions that he could not articulate or understand. The constant barrage of fear made it difficult for him to confront his memories directly, leading him to retreat further into avoidance behaviors that only deepened his emotional struggles. The memories of the assault loomed over him, reinforcing his sense of danger; he often felt that the fear associated with those recollections was as immediate as the original experience, as if he were still trapped in that moment of violence. Once those memories surfaced, the sense of threat sharpened, filling him with a visceral urgency that made him hyper-aware of his surroundings, as though he were still in the midst of the attack. This persistent sense of threat kept his memories activated, making it feel as though he was constantly reliving the event, unable to escape the emotional weight it carried. In those moments, the memories would flood back, vivid and unrelenting, driving him to retreat further into his routines, convinced that isolation was his only refuge from the chaos. His maladaptive strategies became a self-perpetuating cycle. The more he avoided social contacts-friends and fellow musicians he once cherished-the more isolated he felt. He had learned that by avoiding these interactions, he could sidestep the memories that would surge forth in their presence, but this strategy only reinforced his feelings of isolation and kept the memories alive. He noticed that as he withdrew from social interactions, his memories of the assault would surface more frequently, often accompanied by feelings of shame and anger he could neither express nor process. This avoidance not only deepened his emotional struggles but also intensified his memories, making them feel more intrusive and vivid. He had found that by withdrawing from social interactions entirely, he was inadvertently keeping the memories alive, as the lack of distraction made them surface more frequently, echoing in his mind like an unending loop. Eventually, David reached a breaking point. The constant threat he felt had left him on edge, and even the simplest memories of the assault became difficult to keep at bay, surfacing with a vividness that felt unbearable, as if the event was still happening. "When the threat felt this close, he resorted to maladaptive strategies like isolating himself from social situations, believing it was the only way to manage his fear." The weight of his unresolved trauma, coupled with the growing sense of isolation, led him to seek help. "This ongoing threat solidified his memories in a way that made them feel alive and immediate, each recollection pulling him deeper into the past." He hoped to reclaim the joy he once felt in music and life, but he was terrified of confronting the memories that haunted him. This constant sense of threat dictated his actions, compelling him to avoid crowded places and social gatherings, where even benign interactions felt like potential triggers for an emotional collapse. "With every trigger, his sense of threat intensified, making him acutely aware that he was vulnerable to danger, which in turn heightened his anxiety and fear of the past repeating itself." What frightened him most was the thought of reliving the assault, yet he realized that continuing down this path of avoidance was no longer sustainable. "The more he felt that sense of threat, the more he resorted to maladaptive strategies like isolating himself from social situations, convinced that staying away from potential triggers was the safest option." This avoidance of anger became a maladaptive strategy, as he suppressed his feelings to maintain a facade of control, yet in doing so, he found his memories of the assault resurfacing with greater intensity, demanding to be acknowledged. Each of these safety behaviors created an invisible map of avoidance, marking the places he could no longer go without triggering the memories associated with the assault. "The more he avoided confronting these memories, the more he found himself employing maladaptive strategies to cope, escaping into routines that kept the memories at bay but ultimately left them unresolved." As he sat in the therapist's office, he felt a mixture of hope and dread, longing for a way out of his internal prison while fearing what it might take to free himself. "The more he avoided these interactions, the more vivid and intrusive the memories became, as if the act of avoidance itself was a trigger for their resurgence." "Once the memory had surfaced, he couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present - that it had simply moved into his body rather than gone away." "His maladaptive strategies, born out of a desire to escape the weight of those memories, only served to deepen their intrusion, as he found himself constantly revisiting the pain he tried so hard to avoid." Each time he chose to withdraw, he inadvertently laid a path of avoidance that kept the memories fresh in his mind, as if he were perpetually reminded of the trauma he was trying so hard to escape. This ongoing struggle to evade the memories meant that every time they surfaced, they felt more intrusive, as if the very act of avoidance had given them more power and presence in his life. "His withdrawal became a cycle where each time he avoided a social gathering, the memories of the assault surged back with greater intensity, as though his avoidance had given them more power." "To manage the discomfort of these fragmented memories, he began to isolate himself, believing that by avoiding conversations about the trauma, he could keep the memories at bay." "The very act of not confronting his memories through sharing them kept them vivid and fresh, as if he were constantly reminded of the trauma he was trying to escape." "His avoidance behaviors had drawn a map of the event around him: every place he could no longer go and every person he kept at arm's length became a reminder of the trauma, reinforcing his sense of threat."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
David, a 56-year-old musician, had once found joy in the rhythm of life, but a traumatic event had shattered his sense of safety and trust. The assault, which occurred five years ago at a music festival, left him with vivid memories of violence amidst the carefree atmosphere. He could still recall the scent of a specific cologne worn by his attacker, a fragrance that now triggered overwhelming dread whenever he encountered it. It was as if the world had shifted; every instance of blood, whether in a scene from a movie or a minor injury he witnessed, sent him spiraling back to that moment of terror. The mere thought of being in a crowded place where sudden movements could occur made him feel vulnerable, as if danger lurked around every corner.

In the years following the assault, David had developed a rigid routine, confining himself to a limited number of places where he felt somewhat secure, often his home or a quiet corner in a familiar café. Outside of these sanctuaries, he was consumed by irritability, snapping at his wife and friends for minor issues, feeling as though he was perpetually on edge. Authority figures, especially those in uniforms, evoked a deep-seated fear within him, compelling him to avoid interactions at all costs. He had come to believe that expressing anger was a weakness; he never allowed himself to feel or show it, which only added to his internal turmoil. Instead, he suppressed his emotions, a strategy that left him feeling detached and unfulfilled.

David’s memories of the event were fragmented. Some moments were strikingly clear, as if they were etched into his mind, while others remained shrouded in mystery, blank spaces that he could not fill. This inconsistency in his memory led to further confusion and frustration; he often found himself pushing thoughts away before he could fully grasp them, hoping to shield himself from the pain they invoked. He had lost the ability to tell a coherent story of what had happened, both to others and to himself. Each time he attempted to recount the event, he was left with a jumbled narrative that only deepened his feelings of helplessness and loss.

As David navigated his daily life, he encountered triggers that heightened his sense of threat. The smell of cologne would remind him of the assault, making his heart race and his palms sweat. Any sudden movement by those around him would send him into a defensive posture, instantly putting him on guard. It was as if his body had forgotten how to relax; the tension coursed through him, reinforcing his belief that the world was a dangerous place. This heightened threat perception further complicated his ability to engage with his memories, as he often felt overwhelmed by emotions that he could not articulate or understand.

His maladaptive strategies became a self-perpetuating cycle. The more he avoided social contacts—friends and fellow musicians he once cherished—the more isolated he felt. He noticed that as he withdrew from social interactions, his memories of the assault would surface more frequently, often accompanied by feelings of shame and anger he could neither express nor process. This avoidance not only deepened his emotional struggles but also intensified his memories, making them feel more intrusive and vivid.

Eventually, David reached a breaking point. The weight of his unresolved trauma, coupled with the growing sense of isolation, led him to seek help. He hoped to reclaim the joy he once felt in music and life, but he was terrified of confronting the memories that haunted him. What frightened him most was the thought of reliving the assault, yet he realized that continuing down this path of avoidance was no longer sustainable. As he sat in the therapist’s office, he felt a mixture of hope and dread, longing for a way out of his internal prison while fearing what it might take to free himself.

REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette does not convey how triggers lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette lacks a connection between memory and maladaptive strategies, indicating how memories influence coping mechanisms.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette does not show how memories of the trauma contribute to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: There is no indication of how memories are influenced by triggers in the vignette.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not illustrate how perceived threat results in maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not convey that perceived threat influences memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: There is no depiction of how a sense of threat leads to triggers in the vignette.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette does not show how maladaptive strategies impact memory.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not depict how maladaptive strategies are related to triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

vignette_attempts.vignette: David, a 56-year-old musician, had once found joy in the rhythm of life, but a traumatic event had shattered his sense of safety and trust. The assault, which occurred five years ago at a music festival, left him with vivid memories of violence amidst the carefree atmosphere. He could still recall the scent of a specific cologne worn by his attacker, a fragrance that now triggered overwhelming dread whenever he encountered it. These triggers, like the scent of cologne, ignited memories that flooded him with a renewed sense of threat; each encounter felt like a reminder that danger could reemerge at any moment. It was as if the world had shifted; every instance of blood, whether in a scene from a movie or a minor injury he witnessed, sent him spiraling back to that moment of terror. The mere thought of being in a crowded place where sudden movements could occur made him feel vulnerable, as if danger lurked around every corner. Each time he felt that vulnerability rise, it pulled memories of the assault to the forefront of his mind, as if his body was reminding him of the danger he had experienced. In the years following the assault, David had developed a rigid routine, confining himself to a limited number of places where he felt somewhat secure, often his home or a quiet corner in a familiar café. This avoidance of wider spaces and social situations had inadvertently created a web of triggers; every familiar corner became a reminder of what he had lost, reinforcing his isolation while also keeping the memories close to the surface. Outside of these sanctuaries, he was consumed by irritability, snapping at his wife and friends for minor issues, feeling as though he was perpetually on edge. Authority figures, especially those in uniforms, evoked a deep-seated fear within him, compelling him to avoid interactions at all costs. The sense of threat that accompanied these encounters was palpable; he felt that any interaction could lead to a resurgence of the trauma, reinforcing his need to escape even the slightest confrontation. He had come to believe that expressing anger was a weakness; he never allowed himself to feel or show it, which only added to his internal turmoil. Instead, he suppressed his emotions, a strategy that left him feeling detached and unfulfilled. David’s memories of the event were fragmented. Some moments were strikingly clear, as if they were etched into his mind, while others remained shrouded in mystery, blank spaces that he could not fill. This inconsistency in his memory led to further confusion and frustration; he often found himself pushing thoughts away before he could fully grasp them, hoping to shield himself from the pain they invoked. He had lost the ability to tell a coherent story of what had happened, both to others and to himself. This fragmentation of memory was compounded by his avoidance; the more he steered clear of discussing the event, the more intense and disjointed the memories became, almost as if they were waiting to break free and overwhelm him. Each time he attempted to recount the event, he was left with a jumbled narrative that only deepened his feelings of helplessness and loss. As David navigated his daily life, he encountered triggers that heightened his sense of threat. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, amplifying his anxiety and making him hyper-aware of his surroundings." The smell of cologne would remind him of the assault, making his heart race and his palms sweat. Any sudden movement by those around him would send him into a defensive posture, instantly putting him on guard. It was as if his body had forgotten how to relax; the tension coursed through him, reinforcing his belief that the world was a dangerous place. This heightened threat perception further complicated his ability to engage with his memories, as he often felt overwhelmed by emotions that he could not articulate or understand. The constant barrage of fear made it difficult for him to confront his memories directly, leading him to retreat further into avoidance behaviors that only deepened his emotional struggles. The memories of the assault loomed over him, reinforcing his sense of danger; he often felt that the fear associated with those recollections was as immediate as the original experience, as if he were still trapped in that moment of violence. This persistent sense of threat kept his memories activated, making it feel as though he was constantly reliving the event, unable to escape the emotional weight it carried. His maladaptive strategies became a self-perpetuating cycle. The more he avoided social contacts—friends and fellow musicians he once cherished—the more isolated he felt. He had learned that by avoiding these interactions, he could sidestep the memories that would surge forth in their presence, but this strategy only reinforced his feelings of isolation and kept the memories alive. He noticed that as he withdrew from social interactions, his memories of the assault would surface more frequently, often accompanied by feelings of shame and anger he could neither express nor process. This avoidance not only deepened his emotional struggles but also intensified his memories, making them feel more intrusive and vivid. He had found that by withdrawing from social interactions entirely, he was inadvertently keeping the memories alive, as the lack of distraction made them surface more frequently, echoing in his mind like an unending loop. Eventually, David reached a breaking point. The constant threat he felt had left him on edge, and even the simplest memories of the assault became difficult to keep at bay, surfacing with a vividness that felt unbearable, as if the event was still happening. "When the threat felt this close, he resorted to maladaptive strategies like isolating himself from social situations, believing it was the only way to manage his fear." The weight of his unresolved trauma, coupled with the growing sense of isolation, led him to seek help. "This ongoing threat solidified his memories in a way that made them feel alive and immediate, each recollection pulling him deeper into the past." He hoped to reclaim the joy he once felt in music and life, but he was terrified of confronting the memories that haunted him. What frightened him most was the thought of reliving the assault, yet he realized that continuing down this path of avoidance was no longer sustainable. This avoidance of anger became a maladaptive strategy, as he suppressed his feelings to maintain a facade of control, yet in doing so, he found his memories of the assault resurfacing with greater intensity, demanding to be acknowledged. Each of these safety behaviors created an invisible map of avoidance, marking the places he could no longer go without triggering the memories associated with the assault. "The more he avoided confronting these memories, the more he found himself employing maladaptive strategies to cope, escaping into routines that kept the memories at bay but ultimately left them unresolved." As he sat in the therapist’s office, he felt a mixture of hope and dread, longing for a way out of his internal prison while fearing what it might take to free himself. "The more he avoided these interactions, the more vivid and intrusive the memories became, as if the act of avoidance itself was a trigger for their resurgence." "Once the memory had surfaced, he couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into his body rather than gone away." "His maladaptive strategies, born out of a desire to escape the weight of those memories, only served to deepen their intrusion, as he found himself constantly revisiting the pain he tried so hard to avoid."
